title: Fact vs opinion
blurb: Sort any sentence into fact or opinion with one test, including the tricky ones with numbers, experts and mixed claims.
question: A health-fair flyer says, “Last year, nurses screened 640 residents for high blood pressure,” and then, “The fair is easily the most valuable event on the city calendar.” Which sentence is a fact, which is an opinion, and how can you prove it on test day?

teach.h: One test: can it be checked?
teach.body: Formally, a fact is a statement that can be verified, proven true or false by evidence such as observation, measurement, records or reliable sources. An opinion is a statement of belief, feeling, judgment or value that cannot be proven, so reasonable people may disagree. Plain English: if a ruler, a record or a photo could settle the argument, it is a fact. If two people could see the same evidence and still disagree, it is an opinion.

children.label: FACT
children.sub: Even if the claim turns out false

teach.caption: Check every word before you decide: one judgment word anywhere in the sentence is enough to make it an opinion.

teach.h: Fact and opinion side by side

rows.label: Can it be wrong?
values: It is agreed with or not

teach.caption: A false fact is still a factual claim, because it can be checked and shown to be wrong.

head: Signal family
Examples
rows: best, worst, important, terrible, unfair, too, better
I believe, I think, I feel, in my view, it seems
teach.caption: Signal words are clues, not proof. Always apply the core test: could evidence settle it?

teach.h: Scenario: Maya reads a health-fair flyer
teach.body: Maya, a nursing applicant, practices on this flyer. “(1) The Westbrook Health Fair has been held in Lincoln Park every May since 2015. (2) Last year, 1,150 residents attended, and nurses screened 640 of them for high blood pressure. (3) The fair is easily the most valuable event on the city calendar. (4) Free screenings run from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. (5) Every adult in Westbrook should make time to attend. (6) The fair, a real bargain, costs the city $18,000.”

items: Sentence 1: a place and a start year. Park records could confirm it, so it is a fact.
Sentence 2: attendance and screening counts. Sign-in sheets could check them, so it is a fact.
Sentence 3: “most valuable” is a judgment. No record can prove it, so it is an opinion.
Sentence 4: posted hours can be checked, so it is a fact.
Sentence 5: “should” tells readers what to value, so it is an opinion.
Sentence 6: the $18,000 cost is checkable, but “a real bargain” is a judgment, so the sentence mixes fact and opinion.

teach.note: When a question asks for “a statement of opinion,” a mixed sentence like 6 counts, because part of it cannot be proven.

teach.body: Numbers do not make a sentence a fact: “At $18,000, the fair is a bargain” contains a number and is still an opinion. A false statement is not an opinion: it is a factual claim that evidence shows is wrong. An expert's judgment is still opinion, though more credible. And statistics can be facts while an interpretation of them (“this proves the program is a waste”) is opinion.

head: Sentence
Verdict
Why
rows: A cardiologist: “This is the best diet.”

teach.text: The classic HESI A2 traps: picking a sentence because it contains a number (numbers can sit inside opinions), calling a false statement an opinion (it is a false fact), and missing the single judgment word, such as “too,” “better” or “should,” that turns an otherwise factual sentence into an opinion.

items: Fact: can be verified or disproved by evidence. Opinion: belief, feeling, judgment or value.
A false statement is still a factual claim, not an opinion.
Signal words: best, should, important, I believe, probably, everyone knows.
Numbers and experts do not turn an opinion into a fact.
One judgment word makes a sentence an opinion (or a mixed statement).

summary: You can now classify any sentence as fact or opinion by asking whether evidence could settle it. You can also handle the HESI A2 traps: numbers inside opinions, false facts, expert opinions and mixed sentences.

A.q: Which of the following sentences from a hospital newsletter is a statement of opinion?
options: The cafeteria now opens at 6:30 a.m. on weekdays.
Our parking garage holds 420 cars and 12 vans.
The renovated lobby feels far more welcoming.
Visiting hours were extended by one hour in March.
A.why: “Far more welcoming” is a judgment about how the lobby feels. No record or measurement can prove it, so it is an opinion.

whyNot.0: Opening times can be checked against the posted schedule, so this is a fact.
whyNot.1: Garage capacity can be counted and verified, so this is a fact.
whyNot.3: A change in visiting hours can be confirmed from hospital policy records, so this is a fact.

A.q: “In 2023, the county spent $4 million on a larger, unnecessary clinic wing.” Which word or phrase makes this sentence an opinion?
options: larger
unnecessary
spent
clinic wing
A.why: “Unnecessary” judges the wing's value; people could reasonably disagree, and no evidence can settle it. That one word makes the sentence an opinion.

whyNot.0: “Larger” compares size, which can be measured in square feet, so it is checkable.
whyNot.2: Whether the county spent money is a matter of budget records.
whyNot.3: Whether the county built a clinic wing is an observable event that records can confirm.

A.q: A pamphlet states, “The human heart has five chambers.” How should a reader classify this statement?
options: An opinion, because the statement is untrue
An opinion, because it reflects a belief
A mixed statement of fact and judgment
A factual claim, because it can be checked
A.why: A fact is a statement that can be proven true or false. This one can be checked and shown to be false, so it is a false factual claim, not an opinion.

whyNot.0: Being untrue does not make a statement an opinion. A false statement is still a factual claim.
whyNot.1: The sentence states a countable feature, not a belief or value judgment.
whyNot.2: There is no judgment word in the sentence; every part of it can be checked.

B.q: A letter to the editor about new bike lanes includes the sentences below. Which sentence presents a verifiable fact and an opinion together?
options: The lanes, a sensible investment, cost the city $210,000.
Collisions on Elm Avenue fell from 31 to 17 in one year.
Clearly, every street in town deserves the same lanes.
The city painted 3 miles of new lanes on Elm Avenue in May.
B.why: The $210,000 cost can be checked in budget records, but “a sensible investment” is a judgment. The sentence mixes a fact with an opinion.

whyNot.1: Collision counts can be verified in traffic records; there is no judgment word, so it is purely a fact.
whyNot.2: This is purely an opinion (“deserves”); it contains no checkable fact to pair with it.
whyNot.3: Length, location and date can all be verified, so this is purely a fact.

B.q: A report states, “Hand-sanitizer use on Ward 4 rose 40% after new dispensers were installed.” A staff memo adds, “These numbers prove the dispensers were a brilliant idea.” Which choice correctly classifies the memo's sentence and explains why?
options: A fact, because it is based on a measured statistic
An opinion, because it judges what the data mean
A fact, because the 40% rise can be verified
An opinion, because it refers to a percentage
B.why: The 40% rise is a fact, but calling the dispensers “a brilliant idea” is an interpretation and a judgment of that data. An interpretation of statistics is opinion.

whyNot.0: Resting on a statistic does not make a judgment checkable; “brilliant idea” still cannot be proven.
whyNot.2: The report's 40% figure is verifiable, but the memo's sentence goes further and judges it.
whyNot.3: The classification is right but the reason is wrong: percentages can appear in facts or opinions. The judgment word is what matters.

B.q: In a podcast, Dr. Lena Ortiz, a board-certified dermatologist, says, “Mineral sunscreens are the smartest choice for teenagers.” Which choice correctly classifies her statement and explains why?
options: A fact, because a qualified expert said it
A fact, because sunscreen use can be studied
An opinion, though from a credible source
An opinion, because podcasts are not reliable
B.why: “Smartest choice” is a value judgment. An expert's opinion is more credible than a stranger's, but it is still an opinion.

whyNot.0: Expert status adds credibility, not proof. A judgment stays an opinion whoever says it.
whyNot.1: Sunscreen can be studied, but “smartest” is a judgment that studies cannot settle.
whyNot.3: The label is right but the reason is wrong: the medium does not decide it. The judgment word “smartest” does.

C.q: A clinic leaflet reads: “Our nurses gave 2,300 flu shots last October. At 2,300 shots, October was our most impressive month. Next year, demand will probably be higher still. Every family in Riverside should get vaccinated.” Which sentence from the leaflet is a statement of fact?
options: At 2,300 shots, October was our most impressive month.
Next year, demand will probably be higher still.
Every family in Riverside should get vaccinated.
Our nurses gave 2,300 flu shots last October.
C.why: The number of shots given in October can be checked against clinic records, and the sentence contains no judgment word. It is a fact.

whyNot.0: This contains the same number, but “most impressive” is a judgment, so the sentence is an opinion.
whyNot.1: “Probably” signals a guess about the future, which cannot be verified now.
whyNot.2: “Should” tells readers what is right to do, which is a value judgment.

C.q: “The Maple Street pharmacy, which has the friendliest staff in Dayton, stays open until 11 p.m.” Which part of this sentence could be verified?
options: That the pharmacy stays open until 11 p.m.
That the staff are the friendliest in Dayton
That the pharmacy is a better choice in Dayton
That the staff are friendly to every customer
C.why: Closing time can be checked against posted hours. This is the factual part of a mixed sentence.

whyNot.1: “Friendliest” is a judgment that people could reasonably dispute.
whyNot.2: The sentence never makes this claim, and “better choice” would be a judgment anyway.
whyNot.3: The sentence does not say this, and how friendly staff seem is a matter of opinion.

C.q: An article claims, “Everyone knows that night-shift work ruins a nurse's sleep.” Which choice best explains why this is a statement of opinion?
options: It describes a health effect that research has measured
It mentions night shifts, which vary between hospitals
It generalizes about all people and judges an effect
It could be false, and false statements are opinions
C.why: “Everyone knows” is a sweeping generalization, and “ruins” is a judgment word. Both are opinion signals, and the claim as worded cannot be proven.

whyNot.0: If the sentence reported a measured effect, it would be a fact; as written it reports what “everyone knows.”
whyNot.1: Variation between hospitals is outside the sentence and does not decide whether it is fact or opinion.
whyNot.3: False statements are false facts, not opinions, so this reasoning is the classic trap.

reteach.title: The referee test
reteach.question: Picture two friends arguing. Could a referee with a tape measure, a record book or a replay settle it? That is the whole difference between a fact and an opinion.

blocks.body: Jasmine says the gym opens at 6 a.m.; Leo says 7 a.m. A referee checks the posted hours and the argument is over: that was a fact. Now Jasmine says the gym is the best in town; Leo disagrees. The referee can look at everything and still cannot declare a winner: that was an opinion. Even if Jasmine was wrong about 6 a.m., her claim was still a fact, just a false one.

steps.label: Is there a judgment word?
steps.sub: best, should, too, terrible, I think

steps.label: Decide
steps.sub: Settled by evidence = fact; never settled = opinion

blocks.text: The referee does not care who is speaking or whether numbers are involved. A famous doctor saying “the best diet” and a fan saying “$60 is a steal” are both still opinions.

explain.body: A fact can be proven true or false using observation, measurement, records or reliable sources. Dates, counts, places, prices and published results are typical facts. A fact can be wrong: a false fact is still a factual claim.

test.q: Which statement from a school brochure is a fact?
options: The nursing lab was built in 2021 with 24 beds.
The nursing lab is the finest in the state.
Students will probably love the new nursing lab.
The nursing lab is too small for a busy program.
test.why: A build year and a bed count can be checked in school records. There is no judgment word.

whyNot.1: “Finest” is a judgment word; no record can prove it.
whyNot.2: “Probably” and “love” signal a guess about feelings, which is opinion.
whyNot.3: “Too small” is a judgment; one reader's “too small” is another's “just right.”

explain.body: Opinions express belief, feeling, judgment or value. Watch for judgment words (best, worst, important, unfair, too), should words (should, ought, must), feeling verbs (I believe, it seems), guesses (probably) and generalizations (everyone knows).

test.q: “The new triage system, introduced in June, cut average wait times by 12 minutes, which is too modest a gain.” Which word or phrase signals the opinion in this sentence?
options: introduced
too modest
12 minutes
average
test.why: “Too modest” judges whether the gain was big enough, which people could reasonably dispute.

whyNot.0: When a system was introduced can be checked in hospital records.
whyNot.2: A measured change in minutes can be verified from wait-time data.
whyNot.3: An average is a calculated statistic, which is checkable.

explain.body: A number does not make a sentence a fact: “At $60, the class is a steal” is opinion. A false claim does not make a sentence an opinion: “The clinic has 42 beds” when it has 40 is a false fact. Classify by checkability, never by whether a number appears or whether the claim is true.

test.q: Which sentence is an opinion even though it contains a statistic?
options: The study followed 1,200 adults for five years.
In 2024, 18% of patients returned the mailed survey.
The survey had 300 questions across 12 pages.
With 85% satisfied, the clinic is a model for all.
test.why: The 85% figure could be checked, but calling the clinic “a model for all” is a judgment. The statistic sits inside an opinion.

whyNot.0: Sample size and study length can both be verified, so this is a fact.
whyNot.1: A return rate for a given year is a checkable statistic with no judgment word, so this is a fact.
whyNot.2: The number of questions and pages can be counted, so this is a fact.

explain.body: An expert's judgment (“the best treatment”) is still opinion, though a more credible one. Many sentences mix a checkable detail with a judgment: “The 2019 clinic, a disgrace to the city, closed in May.” Split them: the date is fact, “a disgrace” is opinion.

test.q: A news story quotes a hospital's chief nursing officer: “Our 12-hour shift schedule is the fairest system for staff.” How is this quotation best classified?
options: A fact, because an official stated it
A fact, because shift length is measurable
An opinion offered by a credible source
A misconception the story then corrects
test.why: “The fairest system” is a value judgment. The speaker's authority makes it credible, but it remains an opinion.

whyNot.0: Who says a judgment does not make it provable.
whyNot.1: Shift length is measurable, but “fairest” is the claim being made, and fairness cannot be proven.
whyNot.3: Nothing in the stem shows the story correcting a commonly held false belief.
